newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: German heating oil sales dip 1.9 pct in first half.
newsitem.headline: German heating oil sales dip 1.9 pct in first half.

text.p: This year's mild winter resulted in a 1.9 percent decline in German heating oil sales, according to figures from the German oil industry association (MWV).
"We had a harsher winter last year, so there was more filling of tanks than this year," an MWV spokesman said on Thursday.
Sales dipped by 1.9 percent to 18.74 million tonnes in the first half of the year compared with the same period in 1996, the German Oil Industry Association said.
A number of German traders say the figures reflect their own experience of low sales rates.
"We're somewhat behind our planned sales volumes for the year so far," said one.
By contrast, diesel sales rose by 2.7 percent to 12.63 million tonnes in the first six months of the year, leaving total gas oil sales almost identical to those of the first half of 1996.

The decline of heating oil sales has been by no means even. The year began reasonably well with some four million tonnes sold in January, but volumes then tailed off to below three million tonnes per month, except in April and June.
Traders noted business soared in June as the weakness of IPE gas oil futures and a temporary dip of the dollar coincided.

However, since June, demand has fallen off sharply. Many traders say volumes in July have been very low as the dollar has sharply appreciated against the mark. The dollar has been strengthening steadily since late last year.

German heating oil users had become accustomed to steadily declining prices, particularly in mark terms, since the peaks related to the Gulf War in 1991. By mid-1995, prices in Frankfurt, for example, had dipped to a DM27-28 range, some 20 percent lower than in mid-1992.

Current dollar prices are within the same range as in July 1995 and 1996, after a sharp spike last autumn and over New Year, but the steady rise of the dollar versus the mark has ensured that the prices in marks are now at their highest levels in almost five years. -- Philip Blenkinsop, Amsterdam newsroom +31 20 504 5004
